evidence.claims: Checked claims against results.txt: the whitepaper title (paper/whitepaper.md:1) says 'a policy trained on the mean fog is unsafe half the time' but results.txt gives 0.3446 for the mean-alpha policy; the 0.5000 is the median-alpha policy. README.md:3 says a bright-calibrated extinction 'underestimates a dark target's range by up to 29%' but results.txt shows -31.4% at r0=45 (whitepaper:16 also omits it). README.md:3 and whitepaper.md:15 claim closed forms match Monte Carlo to +-0.001, but the median row is 0.5000 vs 0.5012 (0.0012). README.md:10 'about 20 s' vs 4.4 s measured. Limits are stated (stylised, no lidar data) and correct for the rest.
evidence.fitness: A researcher building a lidar sim-to-real study could reuse the closed form and the calibration-transfer observation, but the nearest prior work is not cited: Bijelic et al. 2018 'A Benchmark for Lidar Sensors in Fog' (IV) and Hahner et al. 2021 'Fog Simulation on Real LiDAR Point Clouds for 3D Object Detection in Adverse Weather' (ICCV), which simulate exactly a fog-attenuated lidar from clear-air data with a physical model including backscatter; Kim, McArthur & Korevaar 2001 (SPIE) for NIR fog extinction. The Lambert W solution of a range equation with exponential loss is textbook (the rain-twin sibling uses the same form). Results (1)-(3) are direct algebra from the model; only (4) is a non-obvious observation, and it is a single geometry. Not near a publishable contribution under research/CLAUDE.md's PhD+ bar.
evidence.domain: Range equation for an extended Lambertian target (1/r^2, two-way Beer-Lambert) is right. Departures a lidar/fog practitioner would flag: (a) alpha = 3.912/V is Koschmieder's 2% threshold, while 'meteorological visibility' in WMO practice and in the lidar fog benchmarks is MOR at 5% contrast, alpha = ln(20)/MOR ~ 2.996/MOR, a 31% different extinction for the same V (model.py:8, README); (b) visible-band extinction applied unchanged at 905/1550 nm with no Kim/Kruse wavelength term and no mention in Limitations; (c) the dominant real fog failure of lidar, near-range backscatter clutter and pulse broadening, is excluded (stated); (d) lognormal episode fog and its sigma are not tied to any visibility climatology. Acceptable as a stylised note, not sign-off grade.

verdict: Does not meet the bar (verification 2, claims 2, median 2). The arithmetic is right: every number checked (uniform ranges, elasticities, violation probabilities, speed cost, the fog-bank table) reproduces exactly from an independent bisection/NormalDist script, and the experiment reruns byte-identical. But the paper's title misattributes the 50% violation rate to the mean-fog policy (it is the median; the mean gives 34.5%), two README/paper figures are misquoted (29% vs 31.4%, +-0.001 vs 0.0012), the fog-bank function behind the only non-obvious result survives a seeded bug, and a lidar-in-fog researcher would note the uncited nearest work (Bijelic 2018, Hahner 2021), the Koschmieder-2% vs WMO-MOR-5% convention and the missing NIR wavelength term. A correct, clean stylised note, well short of the PhD+ research bar.
